note: Nestor's decision store had 437 rows, all drafts written by agents proposing to an operator who had never sealed one. The first instinct was to mine agent transcripts for moments the operator said yes. The operator rejected that framing in one sentence: 'each time I have said yes and followed something to production I have committed it or pull request or merged it.' scripts/git_decisions/ was built to that instead -- inventory.py surveys every repository on the box and emits a manifest ordered by how much a person would be asked to read, extract.py turns operator commits and non-robot merges into draft pairs, run_all.py walks the manifest with --stop-after and --resume. 22 repositories, 654 drafts, every one a draft. The operator then sealed 26 by hand in the UI.

decisions.question: Where does a record of what a person actually decided already exist?
decisions.commitment: In git. A commit is a decision the operator made and then acted on; a merged PR is one they decided twice, once to write and once to accept. Both are already durable, already attributed, already timestamped, and already survive the tool that produced them. Mine those, not conversation logs.
decisions.why: A transcript records what was discussed, which includes every option considered and discarded, every hedge, and every thing an agent proposed that the operator ignored rather than refused. Extracting decisions from it means inferring which sentences were binding -- and the inference is the whole difficulty. Git has already done that filtering: the operator's own hand moved the code. Reading a transcript asks 'did they mean this?'; reading a merge says 'they shipped this.' The second question does not need answering.

decisions.question: In what order should 22 repositories be extracted?
decisions.commitment: Smallest first, by the number of decisions a person would be asked to read. The first rung was three -- a number you can read in full and say 'yes, that is what I decided.' Every later rung is judged against a shape already confirmed by eye, and --stop-after exists so the run can be halted to think.
decisions.why: The failure this avoids is finding out the extraction shape is wrong at rung twenty-two, holding 537 rows, with no practical way to check any of them. Confidence in a pipeline is built at a scale a human can actually audit, and then spent at a scale they cannot. Ordering by size is the cheapest way to put the auditable rung first; the alternative -- starting with the interesting repository -- puts the largest unverified batch at the front.

decisions.question: May the pipeline seal anything, given it is reading decisions the operator demonstrably made?
decisions.commitment: No. Every row every rung writes is a draft. That a commit proves the operator decided something in the past does not make an agent's paraphrase of it a thing they have confirmed -- the extraction is a proposal about what the commit meant, and the covenant governs proposals regardless of how good the evidence behind them is.
decisions.why: This is the most tempting exception the seat will meet, because the evidence really is strong: the operator did merge that PR. But the row is not the merge, it is a sentence an agent wrote about the merge, and the operator sealing 26 of 654 by hand is the measure of how often the paraphrase was worth keeping. Had the pipeline sealed on the strength of its source, it would have asserted 654 confirmations from 654 pieces of evidence for something else.

decisions.question: What happens when a re-extraction is run over a store somebody has started reviewing?
decisions.commitment: It refuses unless --force is passed. Ratified rows survive a re-extraction -- this was checked directly, against a VACUUM INTO copy, after an earlier claim that they were destroyed turned out to rest on a plain cp of a live WAL store, which takes a stale main file. What is lost is the review's place: every open decision is re-proposed and the reviewer cannot tell what they had already passed over.
decisions.why: The guard is worth having for the second reason even though the first was wrong, and the message had to be corrected to say so. A warning that overstates the damage teaches the reader to discount it. The durable lesson is separate and larger: never characterize a SQLite store's contents from a file copied out from under a running server -- copy it with VACUUM INTO, or read it through the server that holds the write-ahead log.
